explain.tweet: 2+2=4 was true before any human existed and would stay true if we all vanished. Truths are the kind of thing thought by minds, but not by human ones. Necessary, eternal truths need a necessary, eternal Mind. That is Augustine’s proof of God.
explain.elevator: Think about 2 + 2 = 4. It isn’t ink or brain chemistry — erase every numeral and it’s still true. It isn’t something we invented — it was true before humans existed. So where does it exist? Not in some ghostly realm with no mind, because truths are the sort of thing that are thought, and a mindless realm couldn’t even explain triangles. It has to exist in a mind — but one that’s eternal and can’t fail to exist. That mind, knowing every possible truth, is what we call God.
explain.twoMinute:
Start with something you already believe: some things are true no matter what. Two plus two is four. The angles of a Euclidean triangle add up to two right angles. Those truths were true before any human being existed, and they’d stay true if the universe blew up tomorrow.

Now ask: what *are* they? They’re not physical. You can erase every “2” ever written and arithmetic is untouched. They’re not just words — a German and an ancient Greek can think the exact same thought. And they’re not just ideas in our heads: we discovered them, we can’t change them, and you and I share them rather than each having a private version. Philosophers call things like this — numbers, propositions, universals like triangularity, possibilities — abstract objects. Trying to deny they’re real, or to make them human inventions, ends up using them in the very act of denying them.

So they’re real. But where? Plato said: in a third realm that’s neither physical nor mental. The trouble is that such things couldn’t do anything, couldn’t explain why actual triangles are triangular, and couldn’t be known. And there’s a deeper point: a truth is *about* something — it represents — and representing is what thoughts do. Abstract things exist abstractly only when a mind abstracts them.

So these truths live in a mind. Not a human mind — we come and go, and these truths didn’t wait for us. Not any created mind. It has to be a mind that exists necessarily, that couldn’t not exist. And because all these truths are interlocked — every proposition logically related to every other, infinitely — it has to be one mind grasping them all.

Finally, a mind that exists necessarily can’t have any unrealized potential, or its existence would depend on that potential being actualized. And something with no unrealized potential is one, all-powerful, perfectly good, unchanging, eternal — and knows everything. That’s not a cosmic calculator. That’s God.
explain.eli12:
Imagine you wrote “2 + 2 = 4” on every piece of paper in the world, and then burned all the paper. Would two plus two stop being four? No way! So two plus two equals four isn’t really made of paper or ink.

Is it just in our heads? Well, it was true before any people were born, and it would still be true if all people disappeared. And you and your friend in another country think the very same “two plus two is four,” not two different ones. So it’s not just in anybody’s head.

Some people say it floats around in a special invisible world all by itself. But ideas and truths are things that are *thought*. A truth that nobody is thinking is like a joke nobody tells — hard to say what it would even be.

So here’s the big idea: there must be a Mind that has always existed and can never stop existing, that thinks every true thing all at once. That Mind never learned math — it always knew it. And a mind like that, which can’t be missing anything, would also be all-powerful and perfectly good. That’s what people mean by God.
whiteboard: Write “2 + 2 = 4” and “Snow is white / Schnee ist weiss.” Ask: if I erase these, does the truth disappear? Label the category: ABSTRACT OBJECTS (universals, propositions, numbers, possible worlds).

Draw three boxes: NOMINALISM (only words), CONCEPTUALISM (human-made), REALISM (real, not material, not human-made). Cross out the first two with one-line reasons: regress + words are universals; shared concepts + psychologism refutes itself.
Under REALISM, draw three branches: PLATONIC (third realm), ARISTOTELIAN (in things + finite minds), SCHOLASTIC (in things + finite minds + necessary mind).

Cross out PLATONIC: write “inert — can’t explain or be known,” “Third Man,” “animality neither rational nor not,” “trees = mirror images.” State the key thesis: nothing is abstract without abstraction, so abstract objects need a mind.
Cross out ARISTOTELIAN-only: list the four hard cases — possibility with no world, unicorns, propositions true with no minds, necessary truths. Write “finite minds = contingent” next to them.
Circle SCHOLASTIC → “at least one NECESSARY INTELLECT.” Draw a web of connected nodes (universals, propositions) to show the interlocking system; write “infinite” and “one mind grasps all.”
Draw an arrow: NECESSARY → PURELY ACTUAL (else it depends on some potential being actualized). Cite Chapter 1.
From PURELY ACTUAL, fan out arrows: ONE, OMNISCIENT (no potential to learn), OMNIPOTENT, GOOD, IMMUTABLE, IMMATERIAL, ETERNAL. Write GOD at the end.
In a corner, list the four objections with one-word answers: “concrete?” → begs question; Leftow → entailment ≠ dependence; Grim → proves too much; Coffey → false choice.
explain.keyAnalogy: **The architect’s blueprints.** Before a building exists, its plan exists in the architect’s mind: real before any brick, about the building (it represents), and relevant to what can be built because the architect has the power to build it. Plans no one thinks of exist nowhere. The Augustinian proof says eternal truths and possibilities are like that — ideas in a mind — but because they are necessary and eternal, the mind holding them must be necessary and eternal too, and because they include every possibility, it must know everything and be able to realize any of it. Use the analogy in three beats: (1) representation lives in minds; (2) necessary representations need a necessary mind; (3) possibilities are real possibilities because the mind that holds them has power. Flag its limit: a human architect’s plans are many, changeable, and learned; God’s ideas are one simple, unchanging act of understanding.

persuade.coreInsight:
The idea that makes the argument click is this: **truths are the kind of thing that are thought.** A proposition is *about* something — it represents a state of affairs — and representing is what minds do. So when someone agrees that 2 + 2 = 4 was true before humans and would stay true without them, they have agreed that there is a truth no human mind supports. Either that truth exists in no mind at all (Platonism, with its inert, unknowable, mindless “aboutness”), or it exists in a mind that is not human and cannot fail to exist.

The argument usually fails to click for one of two reasons. First, people slide between the *sentence* and the *proposition*, and think “2 + 2 = 4” is just a human notation. Hammer the erase-every-numeral point until the distinction lands. Second, people think “it’s just true — it doesn’t need to be anywhere.” Show them that this is not a neutral default but a substantive position (Platonism or brute modal facts) with serious problems of its own. Once both confusions are cleared away, the choice is stark: a necessary Mind, or truths that are thoughts no one thinks.

audiences.startingPoint: Believes physics describes objective reality, trusts mathematics completely, and suspects that anything non-physical is superstition.
audiences.approach: Begin with the argument from science: laws of nature are universal, and physics is written in mathematics. Get agreement that scientific laws are discovered, not invented, and hold where no one is observing. Then ask what the mathematics *is*. Walk through the nominalist and conceptualist exits and show that each undermines the very objectivity science depends on — especially the psychologism argument: explaining our logic by evolution requires objective logic and objective laws of evolution. Only then introduce the mind question, and emphasize that this proof uses no gaps in science at all.
audiences.openingQuestion: Was the inverse-square law of gravity true before anyone discovered it — and if so, what exactly was true?
audiences.avoid: Do not suggest science needs God to fill an explanatory gap, and do not start with Augustine or theology. Keep the conversation on the status of mathematical and scientific truth.

audiences.startingPoint: Already thinks numbers and theorems are real, necessary, and discovered — but happily locates them in a mindless abstract realm.
audiences.approach: You agree on Stage 1 entirely, so spend your time on the Platonic/Scholastic fork. Press intentionality (propositions are *about* things; what else is intrinsically about anything but thought?), inertness (how do you know about objects that affect nothing?), and relevance (why would a third-realm object make something possible?). Then show Stage 2 as the natural completion: the infinite, interlocking structure mathematicians love is exactly what one conceptually omniscient mind would hold.
audiences.openingQuestion: When you prove a theorem, you grasp a truth; what would it be for that same truth to exist without anyone, anywhere, ever grasping it?
audiences.avoid: Do not dismiss Platonism as silly — it is a serious view and your ally against nominalism. Do not overstate: the argument needs the thesis that nothing is abstract without abstraction; argue for it rather than assert it.

audiences.startingPoint: Holds that concepts, logic, and even truth are socially constructed and culturally conditioned.
audiences.approach: Use the psychologism and communication arguments gently and Socratically. Ask how they know that concepts are culturally constructed — and notice that the answer uses concepts (culture, power, history) and standards of argument they expect you to accept as valid. Point out that the fact that they are trying to persuade you shows they believe you can grasp the same thought they do. Once objectivity is admitted, move to where objective truths could live.
audiences.openingQuestion: If our logic is just a product of our culture, is that claim itself just a product of our culture — and if so, why should I accept it?
audiences.avoid: Do not score a quick “self-refuting!” point and walk away; it feels like a trick. Take the insight in their view seriously (our *expressions* of truths are culturally shaped — sentences differ) and show that the sentence/proposition distinction honors it.

audiences.who: Christian who knows only the Kalam or design arguments
audiences.startingPoint: Assumes God-arguments are about the Big Bang or fine-tuning, and has never thought about universals.
audiences.approach: Present this as a completely different kind of argument — non-causal, immune to scientific revisions, and rooted in Augustine. Show how it enriches their understanding of God: God is not just a first cause at the beginning but the eternal ground of all truth, whose intellect holds every possibility. Stress the Stage 2 move to pure actuality, which links it to the classical view of God they may not know.
audiences.openingQuestion: If God had never created anything, would 2 + 2 still equal 4 — and where would that truth be?
audiences.avoid: Do not let them turn it into “God decided math,” which is voluntarism. And do not present it as a proof that wins by piling up Bible verses; it stands on philosophy.

audiences.startingPoint: Knows the contemporary debate — Quine, fictionalism, Benacerraf’s problem, abstract objects as non-spatiotemporal and causally inert — and suspects divine conceptualism is a category mistake.
audiences.approach: Engage the contemporary literature directly. Present the Scholastic view as a serious option in the “God and abstract objects” debate (Welty, Plantinga, Adams, Leibniz). Anticipate the “then they’re concrete” objection and explain the rival, abstraction-based notion of abstractness. Deploy Welty’s six conditions as the evaluative framework; they speak this audience’s language. Be ready for Grim and Leftow.
audiences.openingQuestion: Benacerraf asked how we could know about causally inert abstract objects. Doesn’t locating them in an intellect solve that problem better than any Platonist answer?
audiences.avoid: Do not use the contemporary definition of “abstract” without flagging that the Scholastic defines it differently; the whole exchange turns on that. Do not overclaim that every premise is uncontested — acknowledge the 2,300-year debate, as Feser does.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I get the argument from the Big Bang. But how could math possibly prove God?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Let’s start small. Was 2 + 2 = 4 true before there were any humans?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Sure. Dinosaurs didn’t add, but two dinosaurs and two more were four dinosaurs.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: And if every human died tomorrow and every math book burned, would it still be true?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Obviously. But that’s because it’s just a fact about the world. It doesn’t have to be anywhere.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: It’s a fact about the world, but it’s not a physical part of the world. You can’t find the number two under a microscope, and the numeral isn’t the number — “2” and “II” name the same thing. So what kind of thing is it?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe it’s just a concept humans invented, a useful tool.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: But you just said it was true before humans existed. We discovered it; we can’t vote to change it. And when you and I think about the Pythagorean theorem, we’re thinking the same theorem, not two private ones — otherwise we couldn’t even disagree about it.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Okay, then maybe our brains evolved to think mathematically. Evolution explains it.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Evolution explains why we can *grasp* math. But to tell that story you use genetics, selection pressure, probability — mathematics and logic you expect me to accept as objectively valid. If they were just brain habits, your evolutionary argument would be just a brain habit too.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Fine. Then I’m a Platonist: numbers exist on their own, outside space and time. No God needed.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s a serious view. But those objects can’t do anything. How do you know about something that has no effect on you? And how does it explain why this table is rectangular if it affects nothing?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Maybe mathematical knowledge just doesn’t need causal contact.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Then think about a proposition — “snow is white.” It’s *about* snow. It represents something. What’s the one kind of thing we know of that’s intrinsically about other things?

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Thoughts, I suppose. Words and pictures only mean something because someone means them.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Exactly. So the most natural home for truths is a mind. Nothing exists in the abstract except as abstracted by an intellect. But not a human mind — we showed these truths don’t depend on us.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: What about some advanced alien mind? Or a lot of minds together?

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Any mind that came into existence, or could have failed to exist, has the same problem we do. These truths are necessary. They need a mind that exists necessarily. And since every truth is logically connected to every other, infinitely, it’s one mind grasping the whole web, not a committee.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Even so, you’ve got an eternal mathematician. That’s not the God people pray to.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: Here’s the next step. Something that exists necessarily can’t depend on any potential being actualized, or it would be contingent. So it’s pure actuality. And pure actuality can’t lack anything — so it knows all truths, including what you had for breakfast, and it has all power and is perfectly good. That’s the classical God.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: Doesn’t Cantor’s theorem show there can’t be a set of all truths? Omniscience would be incoherent.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: The same reasoning would show there’s no set of all propositions — yet you can truly say every proposition is true or false. Omniscience only requires that there’s no truth God fails to know, not that the truths form a set. And God’s knowledge isn’t a pile of separate items anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Skeptic
dialogue.line: I’ll have to think about the pure actuality part. But I admit I don’t have a good answer for where 2 + 2 = 4 lives.

dialogue.speaker: You
dialogue.line: That’s the honest starting point. Every alternative either denies what you know about math or leaves truths that no one thinks. The Augustinian says: they’re the thoughts of God.

socratic: If every written “2” in the world were destroyed, would 2 + 2 still equal 4? What does that tell you about what a number is?
When a German says “Schnee ist weiss” and you say “Snow is white,” are you thinking two different thoughts or the same one?
Was it possible for human beings to exist before any human being existed? What made it possible then?
Why do we call a stop sign and a fire truck both “red”? Is there any answer that doesn’t mention redness?
When you and I say the word “red,” are we using the same word or two different words that look alike?
If our logic is just a product of evolution or culture, is the argument for that claim just a product of evolution or culture too?
Can something that affects nothing at all explain why anything is the way it is? Can we know about it?
Can there be animality that is neither rational nor nonrational, existing all by itself as a thing?
What kinds of things are intrinsically *about* other things? Can you name one that doesn’t get its aboutness from a mind?
Could a mind that began to exist be the ground of a truth that was true before it began?
If two minds were both perfect and lacked nothing, what could make them two rather than one?
If a mind knew every possible truth, could it fail to know which possibilities are actual?

traps.trap: Confusing the numeral or sentence with the number or proposition, so the skeptic hears “you’re saying God invented our notation.”
traps.fix: Establish the sentence/proposition and numeral/number distinction explicitly at the start, with the erase-every-token thought experiment.

traps.trap: Presenting it as a causal argument — “God created the laws of math.”
traps.fix: Say plainly that this argument is not about causes. It is about what kind of reality necessary truths have: they are thoughts, so they need a thinker.

traps.trap: Skipping Platonism. Many skeptics will happily be Platonists once you refute nominalism, and you have not addressed them.
traps.fix: Treat the Platonic fork as the heart of the persuasion. Have the inertness, animality, intentionality, and relevance points ready.

traps.trap: Sounding like a voluntarist — “God decided that 2 + 2 = 4.”
traps.fix: Stress that necessary truths are grounded in God’s intellect and nature, which are not arbitrary, and that God could not make logic otherwise.

traps.trap: Stopping at the “cosmic mind” and letting the skeptic say “that’s not God.”
traps.fix: Always carry through Stage 2: necessary → purely actual → one, omniscient, omnipotent, good, eternal. Link explicitly to the Chapter 1 reasoning.

traps.trap: Overwhelming a beginner with all ten arguments for realism.
traps.fix: Pick two or three (mathematics, propositions/communication, possible worlds) and hold the rest in reserve for the objections you actually hear.

traps.trap: Using the word “abstract” in two senses without noticing, so the analytic philosopher accuses you of a category mistake.
traps.fix: Say up front: for the Aristotelian, “abstract” means “grasped by abstraction,” so the same nature can be concrete in things and abstract in a mind.

connections.note: The introduction describes the Augustinian proof as rooted in Neo-Platonic thought, central to Augustine, and defended by Leibniz, while stressing that Feser offers a systematic proof inspired by these thinkers rather than an exegesis of them.

Stage 2 depends directly on Chapter 1: a necessarily existing intellect must be purely actual, and Chapter 1 showed that pure actuality is unique, omnipotent, perfectly good, immutable, immaterial, incorporeal, and eternal. Chapter 1’s account of intellect as grasping universal forms, and its Aristotelian notion of substance, also stand behind Aristotelian realism here. Chapter 1 reaches a divine intellect from the causal side; Chapter 3 reaches it from the side of abstract truths.

The reply to Leftow and to Grim both rely on divine simplicity, which Feser discussed in the Neo-Platonic proof: in a simple God, intellect and nature are one and the many divine ideas are one reality. Both proofs share Neo-Platonic roots.

The pure possibles of this chapter (unicorns and the like) reappear in the Thomistic proof: we can know what a unicorn is without knowing whether any exists, which is the doorway to the essence/existence distinction. Chapter 3 asks where uninstantiated essences and possibilities reside; Chapter 4 asks what gives existence to essences at all.

The rationalist proof leans on this chapter twice. Replying to the objection about the “big conjunctive” proposition of all contingent truths, Feser invokes Scholastic realism: propositions are abstract objects existing only in minds that abstract them, not Platonic entities needing their own explanation. And he notes that numbers, universals, and propositions cannot be offered as necessary but non-divine beings, because Chapter 3 shows they cannot exist apart from a mind — their necessity derives from an infinite mind’s. Chapter 6 identifies the rationalist’s necessary being with this chapter’s necessary intellect.

Chapter 6 argues that whatever is purely actual, simple, or subsistent existence itself exists with absolute necessity, so the necessarily existing intellect of Chapter 3 is one and the same as the God of the other four proofs. Its treatments of unity, simplicity, and necessity (including the reply to conventionalism about necessity, which cites this chapter) deepen Stage 2.

Chapter 6’s account of omniscience explicitly draws on this chapter: by the principle of proportionate causality, every form must exist in God in some way; since nominalism, conceptualism, and Platonism are false (Chapter 3), the only way left is as ideas in an intellect — so God has intellect and knows all states of affairs. Chapter 3’s distinction between conceptual and unqualified omniscience is completed there, and the author-of-a-story analogy there complements the architect analogy here.

Among the common objections to natural theology, Feser notes that the “What caused God?” objection is not even prima facie relevant to the Augustinian proof, because this proof — unlike the others — is not a causal argument.

Against scientism, Feser points to the truths of logic and mathematics, which are necessary and objective yet neither empirical science nor mere conceptual analysis — and cites this chapter for the difficulties facing attempts to deny their necessity or objectivity. Natural theology is shown to be in the same position.

In the capstone, the Augustinian proof is your distinctive non-causal route: it meets skeptics on the ground of mathematics and logic rather than cosmology, and converges with the four causal proofs on one and the same purely actual God.
